claims.text: Conventionally cast eutectic high-entropy alloys have coarse lamellar microstructures and segregated phases.
Rapid quenching immediately after casting produces finer eutectic lamellar spacing.
Rapid quenching refines the lamellar microstructure.
Finer lamellar spacing and a more homogeneous phase distribution improve load transfer between phases.
Rapid quenching suppresses eutectic coarsening during solidification.
Suppressing coarsening produces a nano- to microscale refined eutectic structure.
The refined eutectic structure increases yield strength by hindering dislocation motion.
Continuous, well-bonded phase interfaces reduce stress concentrations that cause premature failure.
Reducing interfacial stress concentrations enhances ductility.
Rapidly quenched material will have statistically significantly higher yield strength than a conventionally slow-cooled baseline.
Rapidly quenched material will have statistically significantly greater elongation to failure than a conventionally slow-cooled baseline.
Conventional slow cooling results in coarse lamellar structures.
Excessive quenching rates can produce residual stresses, undesirable phase transformations, brittleness, or defects.
The effectiveness of rapid quenching depends on alloy composition.

contradictions.description: The initial material is described as an already conventionally cast, coarse-lamellar alloy, while the intervention is described as a post-casting thermal treatment. However, the conditions require quenching from above the eutectic point and the mechanism requires suppressing coarsening during solidification. Those latter descriptions imply remelting or control of the original solidification path, not quenching an already formed as-cast microstructure.
